modules.title: Macramé: Knotted Décor That Sells
modules.overview: Macramé turns ordinary cord into wall art, plant hangers and table pieces using a small set of knots. In this module you will choose the right cord, master six working knots, calculate how much cord a project needs, and finish pieces neatly enough to sell.

lessons.title: Cord types, cord maths and six working knots
objectives: Choose between single-strand, 3-ply and braided cord for a given project
Tie the lark's head, square, half square, double half hitch, overhand and gathering knots
Calculate cord length for a project using a stated allowance rule
Set up a simple, comfortable macramé work station at home

blocks.text: Macramé is a way of making textiles by **knotting** cords instead of weaving or sewing them. Every macramé piece, from a small key holder to a two-metre wall hanging, is built from a handful of knots repeated in patterns. If you can tie six knots evenly, you can make almost everything in this module.

blocks.name: knot
blocks.alt: A single tied knot in a cord
blocks.caption: Every macramé design is just a few knots repeated with even tension.

Best for

blocks.text: Cord thickness is given in millimetres. **3 mm** cord is good for small pieces such as coasters and keyrings. **4 to 5 mm** is the most common size for wall hangings and plant hangers. **6 mm and above** gives a bold, chunky look but uses cord quickly. Buy from craft suppliers or check the rope sellers in your local market, and always feel the cord first: cotton is soft and takes dye; nylon and polypropylene are shiny, slippery and harder to knot evenly.
The six working knots

items: **Lark's head knot**: fold a cord in half, place the loop over the dowel or ring, bring it behind, then pull both ends through the loop. This mounts cords and gives you two working strands from each cord.

**Square knot**: work with four strands. The middle two are filler cords that stay still. Cross the left cord over the fillers and under the right cord; take the right cord under the fillers and up through the left loop; pull. Repeat in mirror image (start from the right). The finished knot lies flat.
**Half square knot**: tie only the first half of the square knot again and again. The knots twist naturally into a spiral.
**Double half hitch**: hold one cord tight across the others as a guide. Wrap each working cord around the guide twice. A row of these makes a raised line, straight or diagonal.
**Overhand knot**: a simple loop pulled tight, used to stop fringe ends or to make decorative bumps.

**Gathering (wrap) knot**: binds a bundle of cords together, used at the top and bottom of plant hangers. Wrap a separate cord tightly around the bundle, tuck the end through a loop, and pull the loop up under the wraps.

blocks.title: From cord to finished pattern
items: Choose cord and thickness
Mount with lark's heads
Knot rows with even tension
Shape with hitch lines
Finish and trim fringe
blocks.caption: Most pieces follow this order, so practise each stage on a small sampler first.

blocks.text: How much cord to cut

Running out of cord in the middle of a piece is the most common beginner frustration, because joining new cord in the middle rarely looks neat. A widely used starting rule is to allow **about 4 times the finished length for each working strand**. Because a lark's head folds each cord in half, you cut each cord about **8 times** the finished length. Dense knotting such as many square knots in a row uses more cord, so add extra; open, airy designs use less. Keep notes of what you actually used, so your own rule improves with every piece.

blocks.title: Worked example: cutting cord for a wall hanging
blocks.context: For example, Bisi in Ibadan wants a wall hanging that is 60 cm long (from dowel to end of fringe) on a 40 cm dowel, using 16 cords of 4 mm 3-ply cotton.
steps: Working strand allowance: 60 cm x 4 = 240 cm.
Each cord is folded by a lark's head, so cut length = 240 cm x 2 = 480 cm, or 4.8 m per cord.
Total cord: 16 cords x 4.8 m = 76.8 m.
She adds about 10% as a safety margin for mistakes: 76.8 x 1.1 = 84.5 m, so she plans for 85 m.
Cord is sold in rolls of different lengths; she checks the roll label and buys enough to cover 85 m from one batch, so the colour matches.
blocks.result: Bisi buys about 85 m of cord from a single batch and records how much is left over at the end, to adjust her allowance next time.

blocks.title: Tension is the real skill
blocks.text: Even, firm tension makes knots the same size, which is what makes a piece look professional. Hang your dowel at chest height from a clothes rail, door hook or nail, and stand to work. Tape cord ends with masking tape so 3-ply cord does not unravel while you knot.
Your work station

items: A rail, hook or S-hooks on a clothes rack to hang the dowel at chest height.
Sharp fabric scissors, a measuring tape and masking tape.
A comb or pet brush for fringe, and a spray bottle of water to relax kinks.
A notebook or phone note to record cord length, knot counts and time spent; you need these figures later for pricing.

blocks.text: Practise each knot on a short sampler before starting a real piece: mount four cords on a pencil and tie ten square knots, a spiral of 20 half square knots and two rows of double half hitches. Compare the first and last knots. If they look different in size, slow down and pull each knot with the same force.

takeaways: 4 to 5 mm cotton cord suits most wall hangings and plant hangers
Six knots cover nearly every macramé design
Cut each folded cord about 8 times the finished length, then adjust from your own records
Even tension, not speed, is what makes work look professional

lessons.title: Designing and making a layered macramé wall hanging
objectives: Plan a wall hanging on paper with a clear shape and knot sections
Build alternating square knot panels and diagonal hitch lines
Finish a fringe neatly by brushing, cutting and stiffening
Time and record a full piece for costing

blocks.text: A wall hanging is the best-known macramé product and the one buyers most often ask for to decorate living rooms, bedrooms, short-let apartments and event backdrops. A good hanging has a **clear shape**, a **focal section** where the eye rests, and **clean finishing** at the dowel and fringe. In this lesson you plan and make a medium hanging from start to finish.

blocks.name: artist-at-work
blocks.alt: A maker working on an art piece
blocks.caption: Plan the shape first, then build it section by section on the dowel.

blocks.text: Plan before you knot

Draw the hanging on paper at a small scale, for example 1 cm on paper to 5 cm in real life. Mark three zones: the **header** (top 10 to 15 cm, usually a row of hitches or square knots that holds the cords in order), the **body** (the main pattern), and the **fringe** (loose ends, often cut into a V, a curve or a straight line). Write the knot used in each zone. A clear sketch saves cord, because you can count knots and estimate length before cutting.

blocks.title: Three zones of a wall hanging
items: Header: holds cords in order
Body: main pattern and focal point
Fringe: shape and movement
blocks.caption: Decide what each zone does before you cut any cord.

blocks.text: Alternating square knots

The **alternating square knot** pattern is the backbone of many hangings. In row 1 you tie square knots across using strands 1 to 4, 5 to 8, and so on. In row 2 you leave out the first two strands and tie with strands 3 to 6, 7 to 10, and so on, so each new knot sits between two knots above it. Row 3 goes back to the row 1 pattern. The result is a net that can be tight (knots close together) or open (leave a gap of 1 to 2 cm between rows). To form a downward V, drop two strands from each side on every new row.
Diagonal hitch lines

Double half hitches tied over a diagonal guide cord make crisp lines that frame the body. Hold the outermost strand at an angle across the others as the guide. Tie each strand onto it with two wraps. Keep the guide cord pulled tight at the same angle for the whole row, or the line will curve. Two hitch lines meeting in the middle form a diamond, which is a strong focal point.

blocks.title: Worked example: a 45 cm diamond hanging
blocks.context: For example, Halima in Kaduna makes a hanging for a client's bedroom: 30 cm dowel, 12 cords of 4 mm 3-ply cotton, finished length 45 cm plus fringe.
steps: Cut length: 45 cm x 4 x 2 = 360 cm per cord; 12 cords x 3.6 m = 43.2 m, plus about 10% = 47.5 m.
Header: one row of double half hitches across all 24 strands, 3 cm below the dowel.
Body: two diagonal hitch lines from the outer edges meeting in the centre to form the top of a diamond; inside it, three rows of alternating square knots; then two hitch lines closing the diamond.
Below the diamond: a 10 cm spiral of half square knots in the centre four strands as the focal detail.
Fringe: comb out the ends and cut a V shape so the lowest point is 20 cm below the last knot.
She records time: 2 hours 40 minutes of knotting and 25 minutes of finishing.
blocks.result: Halima has a finished piece and real figures (47.5 m planned, about 44 m used, about 3 hours 5 minutes) to use in her costing.

blocks.text: Professional finishing

items: **Dowel**: sand rough ends; you can stain, paint or wrap the dowel in cord. Upcycled options include a straight, dry tree branch, an old broom handle cut to length or a curtain rod off-cut.
**Hanging cord**: tie a separate cord to both ends of the dowel with a few wraps, so the piece hangs level.
**Fringe**: unravel 3-ply cord with your fingers, brush it with a comb, then cut with very sharp scissors. Wet the fringe slightly and let it dry hanging, to straighten it.
**Stiffening**: for a crisp fringe shape, mist it lightly with a mix of water and a little PVA glue or fabric stiffener, then let it dry before final trimming.

blocks.title: Check every row before moving on
blocks.text: A missed knot or a strand used twice becomes obvious once the piece hangs, and is hard to undo many rows later. After each row, count the knots against your sketch and look at the piece from two metres away.

Photograph the hanging against a plain wall in daylight, from straight in front, and once with a person or a plant beside it so buyers can judge its size. Write its measurements in the caption: dowel width, total length and cord colour. Buyers on WhatsApp and Instagram ask for size first, so give it before they ask.

Common colour choices include natural cotton for a calm, modern look, or dyed sections that match a client's cushions. You will learn to dye cotton in Module 4; dyeing finished cord or cutting dyed fabric strips are both possible, but test on a short length first, because dye can make the cord slightly stiffer.

takeaways: Sketch header, body and fringe before cutting cord
Alternating square knots and diagonal hitch lines build most patterns
A level hanging cord and a crisp fringe signal quality
Record actual cord used and time spent on every piece

steps: Sketch a hanging of 30 to 45 cm length with a header, body and fringe, and label each knot.

lessons.title: Plant hangers, table runners and coasters
objectives: Make a four-arm plant hanger that holds a pot safely
Size the hanger's basket to a specific pot
Adapt square knot panels into a table runner or coasters
Check load and safety before a hanger is sold

blocks.text: Plant hangers are practical, quick to make and easy to sell, especially to people in flats with small balconies. Table pieces such as runners and coasters use the same knots on a flat surface. This lesson teaches both, with attention to the one thing a wall hanging never has to do: **carry weight safely**.

blocks.name: potted-plant
blocks.alt: A green plant in a pot
blocks.caption: A hanger is a product that carries weight, so strength matters as much as looks.

blocks.text: Anatomy of a four-arm plant hanger

items: Pass 8 cords through a metal or wooden ring and fold them so the ring sits at the middle: you now have 16 strands.
Tie a gathering knot just below the ring to bind all 16 strands together.
Divide the strands into 4 groups of 4. Each group becomes one arm.
In each arm, tie a section of square knots or half square knot spirals, for example 15 to 25 cm.
Below the arms, form the basket: take 2 strands from one arm and 2 from the next arm and tie a square knot joining them, about 8 to 10 cm below the arm knots. Go all the way round.
Make a second row of joining knots 6 to 8 cm lower, then gather all strands with a second gathering knot and trim the tail.

blocks.title: Building a plant hanger
items: Ring and gathering knot
Four knotted arms
Joining knots form basket
Bottom gathering knot
Load test with pot
blocks.caption: The basket is formed by joining neighbouring arms, then closed with a second gathering knot.

blocks.text: Sizing the basket to the pot

Measure around the widest part of the pot (its circumference). The joined cords must wrap around the pot without slipping. A simple check: the distance between joining knots around the basket, added together, should be close to the circumference. If the gaps are too large, the pot falls through; too small, and the pot sits on top and tips. Always make the hanger with the pot in hand and test the fit before the bottom gathering knot is tightened.

blocks.title: Worked example: hanger for a 15 cm pot
blocks.context: For example, Ada in Port Harcourt makes a hanger for a plastic pot 15 cm across the top, to hang on a balcony hook.
steps: Circumference = 3.14 x 15 cm = about 47 cm.
The basket has 4 joining knots around it, so the space between each pair is about 47 / 4 = about 12 cm.
She ties the first joining row 9 cm below the arms and checks that the pot rim sits inside the cords.
She ties the second joining row 7 cm lower, slides the pot in, and tightens the bottom gathering knot under it.
She lifts the filled pot (soil, plant and water) by the ring for one minute and checks for slipping knots.
blocks.result: The pot sits upright with the cords holding it below the rim. Ada notes the cord length used so she can repeat the size for the next order.

blocks.title: Weight and hooks
blocks.text: A wet pot of soil is much heavier than it looks. Use braided or 4 to 5 mm cotton cord, a solid metal or hardwood ring, and tell buyers to hang it from a ceiling hook fixed into a joist, a solid beam or a wall bracket rated for the load, never from a curtain rod or a plastic hook. Do not hang plants over beds, baby cots or walkways where someone could be hurt if it falls.
Flat pieces: runners and coasters

A **table runner** is a long panel of alternating square knots, worked flat. Instead of a dowel, mount the cords on a temporary stick and remove it at the end, finishing both ends with an overhand-knot fringe. A runner 30 cm wide and 150 cm long on a dining table is a common size, but measure the table: a runner is often about one third of the table's width and hangs over each end by 15 to 30 cm. **Coasters** are small circles or squares, about 10 to 12 cm, made from 3 mm cord. Coil spirals or square-knot squares both work.

blocks.text: Coasters and charms are a smart way to use the off-cuts left from larger pieces. Keep a box for every piece of cord over 40 cm. Selling a set of four coasters made from leftover cord adds income from material you have already paid for.

blocks.title: Wash test
blocks.text: Before you sell a table piece, make one sample, hand-wash it in cool water with mild soap and dry it flat. Check whether it shrinks, loses shape or bleeds colour. Put honest care instructions on the label based on what you saw.

Before delivery, inspect every hanger: knots tight, no frayed cord, ring smooth with no sharp edges, gathering knot tails tucked. Include a small card that says how to hang it and the maximum pot size it was made for.

takeaways: 8 cords through a ring give 16 strands and 4 arms of 4
Size the basket from the pot's circumference and test with the pot
Hangers carry weight: strong cord, strong ring, proper hook
Off-cuts become coasters and charms

quiz.q: Tolu wants a wall hanging 50 cm long. Using the 4 times per strand rule with lark's head mounting, how long should she cut each cord?
quiz.explain: 50 cm x 4 = 200 cm per strand; folded in half, each cord is 200 x 2 = 400 cm, which is 4 m.

quiz.q: Which knot, tied repeatedly, makes a natural spiral?
quiz.explain: Repeating only the first half of a square knot makes the knots twist into a spiral.

quiz.q: Ngozi's square knots are different sizes along the row. What is the most likely cause?
options: Uneven tension when pulling each knot
She mounted cords with lark's heads
quiz.explain: Knot size depends mainly on pulling each knot with the same force. Hang the work at chest height and slow down.

quiz.q: A client's pot is 20 cm across. About how much cord circumference must the hanger basket wrap around?
quiz.explain: Circumference = 3.14 x 20 = about 63 cm, so the joined cords must wrap about that distance.

quiz.q: Which cord is the better choice for a heavy outdoor plant hanger?
quiz.explain: Braided cord is strong and holds its shape under weight; single-strand cotton is softer and weaker.

quiz.q: In row 2 of an alternating square knot pattern, what should the maker do?
options: Use the same four strands as row 1
Skip the first two strands so knots sit between the ones above
quiz.explain: Shifting by two strands makes each new knot sit between two knots above, forming the net pattern.

modules.title: Advanced Surface Decoration
modules.overview: A plain tray, jar, stool or cushion can be transformed by what you put on its surface. This module covers advanced decoupage, decorative paint finishes and repeat patterns with stencils and carved blocks, with the preparation and sealing steps that make the finish last.

lessons.title: Advanced decoupage on wood, glass and metal
objectives: Prepare wood, glass and metal surfaces so decoupage stays stuck
Apply thin napkin, paper and fabric layers without bubbles or wrinkles
Build and sand protective coats for a smooth, durable finish
Choose a sealer that suits how the item will be used

blocks.text: **Decoupage** means decorating a surface with cut-out paper or fabric, glued down and then covered with layers of sealer until the cut-out looks painted on. Beginners glue a picture and stop. Advanced work is different: the edges disappear, there are no bubbles, and the surface is smooth enough to wipe. That result comes from three things: **preparation**, **thin material**, and **many thin coats**.

blocks.name: black-scissors
blocks.caption: Careful cutting and tearing decide how invisible your edges will be.

blocks.text: Prepare the surface

head: Surface
Preparation
Base coat
rows: Raw or old wood (trays, stools, boxes)
Sand with 120 then 180 grit, wipe off all dust with a damp cloth
1 to 2 coats of white or light emulsion or acrylic so prints show true colour
Wash with soap, dry, wipe with methylated spirit to remove grease
None for see-through work; or a light acrylic coat

blocks.text: Choosing and thinning your paper

items: **Printed paper napkins**: very thin, so edges vanish. Peel away the plain white back layers and keep only the printed top layer.
**Rice or tissue paper**: strong but thin; good for large areas.
**Magazine pages and old book pages**: thicker; make them thinner by sealing the front with one coat of sealer, then soaking and gently rubbing paper off the back.
**Printed photocopies**: use laser or photocopy prints; many inkjet prints smear when wet, so seal them first and test.
**Fabric such as ankara**: cut with sharp scissors; stiffen first with diluted PVA so it does not fray.

blocks.text: The application method

items: Tear or cut your design. Torn edges blend into the background better than straight cut edges.
Brush a thin coat of decoupage medium (or PVA glue diluted about 3 parts glue to 1 part water) onto the surface, not the paper.
Lay the paper on, then smooth it from the centre outwards with a soft brush, or press through a sheet of cling film with your fingers to push out air.
Let it dry fully, usually 20 to 30 minutes in Nigerian heat; longer in the rainy season.
Apply a thin top coat of medium over the whole area. Let it dry, then add more coats, each brushed in a different direction.

blocks.title: The coat and sand cycle
items: Apply thin coat
Dry fully
Light wet sand
Wipe clean
Next coat
blocks.caption: Repeating this cycle buries the paper edge until the surface feels smooth.

blocks.text: Burying the edge

After about four coats, sand lightly with fine wet-and-dry paper (for example 400 grit), dipped in water, using very gentle pressure. You are only flattening ridges, not reaching the paper. Wipe clean, let dry, then coat again. Experienced decoupage makers often build up eight to ten coats or more on trays for a glass-smooth feel. If you sand through to the paper, stop, let it dry and add more coats over that area.

blocks.title: Worked example: a napkin decoupage serving tray
blocks.context: For example, Funke in Abeokuta upcycles an old wooden tray (40 x 30 cm) bought cheaply, to sell as a decorative tray for a living room.
steps: Sands the tray with 120 and 180 grit, removes dust, and paints two coats of white emulsion, drying 2 hours between coats.
Uses two printed napkins with a leaf design, peeling off the back plies so only the printed layer remains.
Applies diluted PVA to one half of the tray, lays the napkin, smooths through cling film, then repeats for the other half, overlapping torn edges by 1 cm.
Builds 8 thin coats of water-based varnish over two days, wet-sanding after coats 4 and 6.
Paints the rim and sides in a dark green that matches the leaves, then varnishes those too.
blocks.result: The tray has no visible napkin edges and a smooth, wipeable surface. Funke labels it as decorative, for dry items and wiping only.

blocks.title: Not for food contact or soaking
blocks.text: PVA glue, decoupage medium and most varnishes are not tested as safe for direct contact with food, and decoupage softens if soaked. Do not sell decoupage plates, bowls or cups for eating. Decorate the back of clear glass plates or the outside of jars only, and label items 'wipe clean, do not soak, decorative use'.
Choosing a sealer

For indoor décor, water-based acrylic varnish or polyurethane is easy to use and has low smell. Some clear sealers turn slightly yellow over time, especially oil-based ones, which shows on white backgrounds; test on a sample board and leave it in a sunny window for a few weeks. For outdoor items, choose a sealer labelled for exterior use and expect to reseal. Always read the tin: dry time, recoat time and ventilation instructions differ by brand.
Work in a dust-free corner. A single fly or speck of dust in wet varnish ruins the smooth finish. Cover drying pieces loosely with an upturned clean box, raised on blocks so air can move.

takeaways: Preparation and a light base coat make prints show true colour
Thin paper, torn edges and smoothing from the centre prevent bubbles
Many thin coats with light wet sanding bury the edges
Decoupage is decorative, not food-safe and not for soaking

activity.title: Decoupage sample board and finished piece
steps: Make a sample board: decoupage a napkin and a magazine image side by side on a piece of wood.
Build 6 coats on the board, sanding after coat 4, and note which edge disappears better.
Choose a jar, tin or tray from home and decoupage it using the better method.
Write a care label for it.

lessons.title: Decorative paint effects and faux finishes
objectives: Match paint type to surface: emulsion, acrylic, enamel and chalk-style paint
Create dry brush, colour wash, sponged, distressed and crackle finishes
Mix a homemade chalk-style paint in correct proportions
Plan paint quantities for small items without waste

blocks.text: Paint effects turn cheap or worn objects into pieces that look aged, textured or expensive. A plastic vase can look like stone; a new stool can look like a well-loved antique. The secret is **layers**: a base colour, a contrasting top colour, and a technique that lets some of the base show through.

blocks.name: lower-left-paintbrush
blocks.caption: Most faux finishes use a cheap brush, a sponge and two contrasting colours.

blocks.text: Know your paints

head: Paint
Base
Use on
Clean brushes with
rows: Thinner or kerosene, as on the tin
Furniture, frames, vases; good for distressing

blocks.text: Water-based paints dry quickly, smell less and are easier for a home workspace. Oil-based paints are tougher but need ventilation and solvent clean-up. Never mix water-based and oil-based paint in the same tin.
Five finishes to master

items: **Dry brushing**: dip only the tips of a dry brush in paint, wipe most of it off on paper, then sweep lightly across the surface. Paint catches only on raised parts, highlighting carvings and texture.
**Colour wash**: thin paint with water (for example 1 part paint to 3 or 4 parts water), brush on and wipe with a cloth. Wood grain shows through softly.
**Sponging**: dab a natural or kitchen sponge in a second colour, blot it, then press onto a dry base coat. Rotate the sponge to avoid a repeating mark. Good for a stone look.
**Distressing**: paint a dark base, then a light top coat. When dry, sand edges and corners where natural wear would happen, so the dark colour shows.

**Crackle**: paint a base colour, brush on crackle medium (or a coat of PVA glue, a common substitute), and while it is still tacky, brush a top colour on in one direction. Cracks open as it dries, showing the base.

blocks.title: Distressed vs crackle finish
items: Distressed
Crackle
blocks.caption: Both reveal the base colour, but in different places and with different tools.

blocks.text: Homemade chalk-style paint

Ready-made chalk paint is often imported and costly. A widely shared home recipe mixes **plaster of Paris** with emulsion paint. Stir about **1 part plaster of Paris into 1 part cool water** until smooth with no lumps, then mix that paste into **3 parts emulsion paint**, all by volume. It gives a matt, slightly gritty finish that grips many surfaces and sands easily for distressing. Mix only what you will use in one session, because it thickens as it stands. Seal with clear wax or water-based varnish.

blocks.title: Worked example: chalk-style paint for two side stools
blocks.context: For example, Grace in Jos needs about 750 ml of finished paint to give two small stools two coats each.
steps: Total parts = 1 (plaster) + 1 (water) + 3 (paint) = 5 parts by volume. The plaster powder settles into the water, so the finished paint comes out a little under the total. To be safe she plans for 800 ml.
800 ml / 5 parts = 160 ml per part.
She measures 160 ml plaster of Paris and 160 ml water, stirs to a smooth paste, then mixes it into 480 ml emulsion (3 x 160 ml).
She applies coat 1, lets it dry about 1 hour, and stirs again before coat 2 because the mix thickens.
After distressing edges with 120 grit, she seals with water-based varnish.
blocks.result: Grace has enough paint for both stools with a little left over, and a matt, distressed finish sealed against marks.

blocks.title: Plaster dust and sanding
blocks.text: Plaster of Paris and sanded paint make fine dust. Mix and sand outdoors or near an open window, wear a dust mask, and keep children away. Never pour leftover plaster mix down a sink: it hardens in pipes. Let it set in the container and dispose of it with solid waste.
Faux metal and gilding

A gold or bronze touch on a frame edge, a vase rim or carved details lifts a piece instantly. Use metallic acrylic paint applied with dry brushing, or **gilding**: brush a special size (adhesive), wait until it is tacky as the label directs, press on imitation gold leaf, then brush away the excess with a soft brush. Seal imitation leaf, because it can tarnish.

blocks.title: Always test on a sample
blocks.text: Keep a stack of scrap boards or cardboard. Before any client piece, test the colour pair and technique on a sample. Label the back with paints and steps used, and you build a finish library to show clients.

For small items, a 250 ml tin of emulsion goes a long way; you rarely need a full 4-litre bucket. Buy sample pots or share larger tins with other makers, and record how much each item used so your costing is accurate.

takeaways: Layering a base and a contrasting top colour is the core of faux finishes
Match paint to surface and never mix water-based with oil-based
Homemade chalk-style paint: 1 plaster, 1 water, 3 emulsion by volume
Test finishes on samples and keep a labelled finish library

activity.title: Finish library
steps: Prepare five scrap boards or thick cardboard pieces with a base coat.
Make one sample each: dry brush, colour wash, sponge, distressed and crackle.
Mix a small batch of chalk-style paint and use it for the distressed sample.
Label the back of each sample with colours, products and steps.
activity.evidence: Photo of all five labelled samples side by side

lessons.title: Stencilling and block printing repeat patterns
objectives: Cut a durable stencil with bridges from upcycled plastic film
Stencil cleanly using the off-load and pounce method
Carve and print a simple block on fabric and wood
Plan a repeat pattern so it fits the item exactly

blocks.text: Stencils and printing blocks let you repeat a design many times with the same quality. That is what makes a matching set of cushions, napkins or wall borders possible, and what turns a hobby into production. This lesson covers making the tools from low-cost and upcycled materials, printing cleanly, and planning repeats with simple arithmetic.

blocks.name: making-art
blocks.alt: A person creating a patterned artwork
blocks.caption: A good stencil or block lets you repeat one design cleanly across a whole set.

blocks.text: Making a stencil

items: **Material**: clear acetate sheets, plastic folder covers or cleaned old X-ray film all work. They are thin, waterproof and can be washed and reused. Thick card works for a few prints only.
**Design**: draw a bold, simple shape. Fine lines and tiny gaps clog with paint.
**Bridges**: any closed shape (like the centre of an 'O' or a leaf) needs small strips, called bridges, that hold the inner piece in place. Make bridges at least 3 to 4 mm wide.
**Cutting**: tape the film over the drawing on a cutting board or thick cardboard and cut with a sharp craft knife, turning the board rather than your hand on curves.

blocks.title: Craft knife safety
blocks.text: Always cut away from your body and your other hand, use a metal ruler for straight lines, change blades when they drag, and close or cap the knife between cuts. Keep blades away from children and wrap used blades in tape before throwing them away.
Printing a clean stencil

items: Fix the stencil with masking tape or a light spray of repositionable adhesive so it cannot move.
Load a stencil brush or a piece of dense sponge with a small amount of paint.
**Off-load**: dab most of the paint onto paper towel until the brush is almost dry. Too much paint is the main cause of bleeding under the edges.
**Pounce**: dab straight up and down, building colour in two or three light layers rather than one heavy one.
Lift the stencil straight up, wipe its back, and move to the next position.

blocks.text: Block printing

Block printing uses a raised design that you ink and press down, like a stamp. You can carve **lino** or a **soft rubber carving block** with lino cutting tools, or make a quick block from craft foam glued onto a wooden off-cut. Remember that a block prints in **mirror image**: letters and asymmetrical shapes must be carved reversed. Roll ink or fabric paint thinly with a small roller (a brayer), press the block firmly, and lift straight up.

head: Surface
Paint or ink
Fixing
rows: Fabric paint or textile screen ink
Heat-set with a dry iron as the product label directs
Seal with clear varnish on items that are handled

blocks.text: Planning a repeat that fits

A pattern looks professional when it fits the item evenly, with no half-motif squeezed in at one edge. Measure the item, decide the motif size plus spacing, and divide. If it does not divide evenly, adjust the spacing, not the motif. Mark light pencil or chalk guide lines, or tape a strip of paper with marks along the edge as a registration guide.

blocks.title: Worked example: printing a set of four cushion covers
blocks.context: For example, Chioma in Enugu prints plain cream cotton covers that are 45 cm square, using a carved block whose motif is 7 cm square.
steps: She wants a 1 cm border at each edge, so the print area is 45 - 2 = 43 cm across.
Trying 5 motifs per row: 5 x 7 cm = 35 cm of motif, leaving 43 - 35 = 8 cm for 4 gaps, which is 2 cm per gap.
Five rows gives 25 prints per cover, and 4 covers need 100 prints.
She washes and irons the covers first (new fabric can carry a finish that stops paint soaking in), slips cardboard inside so paint does not pass to the back, and marks a 2 cm grid with chalk.
After 24 hours drying, she heat-sets each cover with an iron as the fabric paint label directs.
blocks.result: Each cover has an even 5 x 5 grid with matching gaps, and the set of four looks identical. She records 100 prints and the paint used for costing.

blocks.title: From idea to printed set
items: Bold simple design
Cut stencil or carve block
Test on scrap fabric
Mark repeat grid
Print, dry, heat-set
blocks.caption: Testing on scrap and marking the grid prevent most wasted pieces.

blocks.title: Use local motifs respectfully
blocks.text: Geometric motifs, local plants and everyday objects make strong, original designs. If you borrow from a traditional pattern such as adire motifs, say so in your product description and do not copy another designer's original work.

Clean stencils and blocks immediately after printing with water for water-based paint, so paint does not dry in fine cuts. Store stencils flat between sheets of paper, and keep each block with a printed sample so you can show clients your pattern range.

takeaways: Upcycled plastic film makes durable, washable stencils
Off-load the brush and pounce in light layers to stop bleeding
Blocks print in mirror image, so carve text reversed
Fit repeats by adjusting gaps, then mark a grid before printing

activity.title: Repeat pattern sample
steps: Design one motif no larger than 8 cm and cut it as a stencil from plastic film.
Choose an item (napkin, tote bag, box lid) and calculate a repeat that fits with equal gaps.
Test the print on scrap fabric or paper.
Print the item and fix the paint as the label directs.
activity.evidence: Photo of the stencil, your written repeat calculation and the finished printed item

quiz.q: Amaka's decoupage napkin edges still show after two coats. What should she do?
options: Add more thin coats with light wet sanding between them
Peel it off and start again
Apply one very thick coat of glue
quiz.explain: Many thin coats with gentle wet sanding gradually bury the edge until it disappears.

quiz.q: A client asks for decoupage dinner plates for daily eating. What is the right answer?
options: Offer decoration on the back of clear glass plates for display, labelled decorative
Use magazine paper instead of napkins
quiz.explain: Decoupage media and most varnishes are not tested as food-safe and soften when soaked, so keep food surfaces undecorated.

quiz.q: Using the recipe 1 part plaster of Paris, 1 part water, 3 parts emulsion, how much emulsion goes with 100 ml of plaster?
quiz.explain: One part is 100 ml, so 3 parts of emulsion is 300 ml.

quiz.q: Which technique highlights only the raised parts of a carved frame?
quiz.explain: A nearly dry brush deposits paint only where it touches raised areas.

quiz.q: Paint keeps bleeding under Bola's stencil. What is the most likely fix?
options: Off-load the brush and pounce in light layers
Use more paint so it covers faster
Use a wider brush with strokes
quiz.explain: Too much paint creeps under edges; an almost dry brush used with up-and-down dabbing gives crisp edges.

quiz.q: A table runner print area is 40 cm. The motif is 6 cm and she wants 5 motifs. What gap fits between them?
quiz.explain: 5 x 6 = 30 cm of motif leaves 10 cm for 4 gaps, which is 2.5 cm each.

modules.title: Concrete, Clay and Mixed Media
modules.overview: Cement, air-dry clay and found objects let you make solid, sculptural décor: planters, candle holders, trinket dishes, wall pieces and framed assemblages. This module teaches correct mixes, moulds from waste containers, safe handling of cement, and how to compose objects into art.

lessons.title: Casting planters and candle holders in cement
objectives: Handle cement safely with the right protective equipment
Mix a sand and cement casting mix in correct proportions and consistency
Make two-part moulds from upcycled containers and release the cast cleanly
Cure, finish and seal cement décor so it lasts

blocks.text: Cement planters, candle holders, bookends and coasters are popular modern décor, and the raw material is sold in every Nigerian building materials market. Strictly, cement mixed with only sand is **mortar**, and with sand plus gravel it is **concrete**; for small décor most makers use a sand and cement mix because fine sand gives smoother surfaces. Everyday speech calls all of it 'concrete', and so will this lesson.

blocks.name: brick
blocks.caption: The same Portland cement used for building can be cast into small décor objects.

blocks.title: Cement can burn skin and eyes
blocks.text: Wet cement is strongly alkaline and can cause chemical burns and dermatitis; the dust irritates eyes, nose and lungs. Wear waterproof gloves (nitrile or rubber), safety goggles, a dust mask when pouring dry powder, and long sleeves. Mix outdoors or in a well-ventilated space. If wet cement gets on skin, wash it off promptly with plenty of clean water; if it gets in the eyes, rinse with clean water for at least 15 minutes and seek medical help. Never mix cement in food containers you will use again for food, and keep children and pets away.
Materials and moulds

items: **Cement**: ordinary Portland cement, sold in 50 kg bags. Buy a small quantity from a seller who splits bags if you only need a few kilograms, and keep it dry, because damp cement forms lumps and becomes useless.
**Sand**: fine, clean sharp sand, sieved through a kitchen sieve or mosquito net to remove stones and leaves.
**Moulds**: two containers, one inside the other, such as a large and small ice cream bucket, yoghurt cups, plastic bottles cut in half, or old food tins. Flexible plastic releases most easily.
**Release agent**: a thin coat of used cooking oil or petroleum jelly on every surface that touches the mix.
**Weights and spacers**: stones or sand to hold the inner mould down, and a cork or short pipe for a drainage hole.

blocks.text: The mix

A practical casting mix for small pieces is about **1 part cement to 2 parts fine sand by volume**. Some makers use 1 to 3 for a coarser, cheaper mix. Add water little by little and stir until it looks like **thick porridge**: it should hold a shape on the trowel but settle when you tap the container. Too wet and the piece is weak, cracks and shrinks; too dry and it will not fill the mould, leaving holes. Mix only what you can pour in about 20 to 30 minutes.

blocks.title: Life of a cement cast
items: Mix and pour: 30 min
Initial set: about a day
Demould gently
Keep damp: about 7 days
Gains strength for weeks
blocks.caption: Cement keeps hardening long after demoulding, as long as it stays damp while it cures.

blocks.text: Casting step by step

items: Oil the inside of the outer mould and the outside of the inner mould.
For a planter, push an oiled cork or short pipe into the centre of the outer mould base to form a drainage hole.
Pour mix into the outer mould to about 2 cm deep for the base, then press the inner mould down onto it and centre it, leaving walls at least 1.5 to 2 cm thick.
Fill the gap between the moulds, tapping the sides firmly for a minute or two to release air bubbles.
Weigh the inner mould down with stones or sand so it cannot float up.
Cover with nylon and leave in shade for about 24 hours, then remove the moulds gently.

blocks.title: Worked example: four small planters
blocks.context: For example, Esther in Abuja wants to cast four planters, each with an outer mould of about 1 litre and an inner mould of about 0.5 litre.
steps: Mix volume per planter = 1.0 - 0.5 = 0.5 litre of wall and base. Four planters need 4 x 0.5 = 2 litres.
Wet mix shrinks in volume compared to the dry ingredients, so she prepares about 2.5 litres of dry material.
At 1 cement : 2 sand, 2.5 litres is 3 parts, so 1 part is about 0.83 litre. She measures about 0.8 litre cement and 1.7 litres sand using a marked 1-litre cup.
She adds water a little at a time until it looks like thick porridge, records the water used, and pours all four in one session.
She demoulds after 24 hours and keeps the planters wrapped in damp cloth inside nylon for 7 days, wetting the cloth daily.
blocks.result: All four planters come out with smooth walls and drainage holes. Her written quantities let her repeat the batch exactly.

blocks.text: Curing and finishing

Cement hardens by a chemical reaction with water, not by drying. If a fresh piece dries out quickly in the sun or harmattan wind, it becomes weak and dusty. Keep it damp and covered for about a week. After that, sand rough edges with wet-and-dry paper, used wet to keep dust down. Fill small holes with a paste of cement and water. Paint with emulsion or acrylic, or leave the natural grey and seal with a clear masonry sealer if you want it water-resistant.

blocks.title: Before planting
blocks.text: New cement can make soil water very alkaline, which some plants dislike. Many makers soak finished planters in water for a few days, changing the water, before planting. Always include a drainage hole, or tell the buyer it is a cover pot for a plastic pot inside.

For candle holders, set a tealight or the empty cup it came in as the inner mould, so the hollow is the right size. Cement does not burn, but never leave lit candles unattended and tell buyers to place holders on a heat-proof surface away from curtains.

Dispose of leftover mix by letting it harden in a container and throwing it out as solid waste. Never rinse cement down drains or into gutters; it sets underwater and blocks them. Rinse tools in a bucket of water and let the sediment settle before pouring the clear water away.

takeaways: Wet cement is alkaline: gloves, goggles and a mask are essential
About 1 cement to 2 fine sand, mixed like thick porridge, suits small casts
Oiled two-part moulds from waste containers make planters and holders
Keep pieces damp for about a week, and never wash cement down drains

activity.title: Cast and cure one planter
steps: Collect two nesting containers and calculate the mix volume needed.
Set up your safety gear and work area, and photograph it.
Mix, pour, tap and weigh down the inner mould.
Demould after 24 hours and cure damp for 7 days, wetting daily.
Sand, seal or paint, and note any cracks or holes and their likely cause.
activity.evidence: Photos of the safety setup, the pour, and the finished planter, plus a curing log with dates

lessons.title: Air-dry clay and homemade cold porcelain décor
objectives: Compare bought air-dry clay with homemade cold porcelain
Shape trinket dishes, beads and wall pieces with pinch, slab and mould methods
Join pieces securely and dry them without cracking
Seal and label clay décor correctly as non-food items

blocks.text: Air-dry clay hardens at room temperature, so you need no kiln. It is ideal for trinket dishes, jewellery dishes, small vases for dried flowers, wall plaques, decorative beads and name tags. Because it is not fired, it stays sensitive to water: this one fact shapes how you finish it and what you tell buyers.

blocks.name: jar
blocks.caption: Air-dry clay suits small dishes and vessels for dry items, not for water or food.

blocks.text: Two clays you can use

blocks.title: Bought air-dry clay vs cold porcelain
items: Bought air-dry clay
Homemade cold porcelain
blocks.caption: Choose by the size and finish the piece needs, and test both.

blocks.text: Making cold porcelain

Cold porcelain is a dough made from **cornstarch** (corn flour) and **white PVA glue**, with a little oil and an acid such as lemon juice or vinegar to help it keep. A commonly used recipe is **1 cup cornstarch, 1 cup PVA glue, 1 tablespoon vegetable or baby oil and 1 tablespoon lemon juice or white vinegar**. Mix everything in a non-stick pot, stir over low heat until it pulls away from the sides as one lump, then turn it out and knead with oiled hands as it cools. Wrap tightly in cling film and store in an airtight container.

blocks.title: Kitchen tools and heat
blocks.text: Use a pot and spoon kept only for crafts afterwards, because glue residue is not food-safe. The dough is hot when it comes off the heat: let it cool enough to handle, and keep children away from the stove. Wash hands after working with clay and glue.
Three ways to shape

items: **Pinch**: roll a ball, push your thumb into the centre and pinch the walls evenly while turning it. Good for small bowls and tealight cups (with a glass insert).
**Slab**: roll clay to an even thickness between two wooden strips about 5 mm thick. Cut shapes with a knife or a cutter, then press texture into them with lace, leaves or a stamp.
**Drape mould**: lay a slab over or inside an upturned saucer or bowl lined with cling film, trim the edge, and let it firm up before removing.

blocks.text: To join two pieces, **score** both surfaces with crosshatched scratches, brush on a little water (or for cold porcelain, a dab of PVA), press together and smooth the seam. Without scoring, joins often separate as the clay dries and shrinks.

blocks.title: Worked example: a set of six ring dishes
blocks.context: For example, Rahila in Makurdi makes ring dishes to sell as gifts in sets of three.
steps: She rolls a slab 5 mm thick between two wooden strips and presses an old lace doily into it for texture.
She cuts six circles using a 10 cm diameter cup as a cutter.
She drapes each circle inside a cling-film-lined saucer so the edges curve up.
She dries them slowly, loosely covered with a cloth, turning them over after the first day so the bottoms dry too; total drying is about 3 days in her room.
She lightly sands edges, paints the rims with gold acrylic, and seals each dish with two coats of water-based varnish.
blocks.result: Six even dishes, packed as two sets of three. Her label says: decorative dish for rings and dry items, wipe with a dry cloth, not for food or water.

blocks.text: Drying without cracks

items: Keep thickness even: thick and thin parts dry at different speeds and crack where they meet.
Dry slowly out of direct sun and fan wind; harmattan air dries surfaces fast, so cover pieces loosely.
Turn flat pieces so both sides dry.
Small hairline cracks can be filled with a paste of the same clay and water (or PVA for cold porcelain), then sanded smooth once dry.
Expect some shrinkage, especially in cold porcelain; make pieces slightly bigger than the size you need.

blocks.text: Sealing and honest labelling

Seal every finished piece with acrylic varnish, water-based polyurethane or a clear sealer to protect it from humidity and handling. Even sealed, air-dry clay is **not waterproof** and is **not food-safe**. Vases for fresh flowers need a glass or plastic tube inside to hold water. Planters need a plastic pot inside. Say this on the label and in your product description, so a buyer is never disappointed.

Costing clay work is mostly about time, because the materials are cheap. Weigh or measure the clay used for one piece, note how long shaping, sanding and painting took, and remember that drying days tie up shelf space, not your hands. Making pieces in batches of six or more, all at the same stage on the same day, cuts the time per piece sharply compared with making one at a time.

blocks.title: Colour in the clay
blocks.text: Knead a little acrylic paint into cold porcelain before shaping to colour it all the way through. Wear gloves to keep your hands clean, and record how much paint you used per ball so colours match across a set.

takeaways: Air-dry clay needs no kiln but is never waterproof or food-safe
Cold porcelain: 1 cup cornstarch, 1 cup PVA, 1 tbsp oil, 1 tbsp lemon juice or vinegar
Score and join; keep thickness even; dry slowly and turn pieces
Seal every piece and label it honestly

activity.title: Clay sample set
steps: Make a half batch of cold porcelain (half a cup each of cornstarch and PVA).
Make one pinch piece, one textured slab piece and one draped dish.
Dry them slowly, recording days to dry and any cracks.
Seal and write an honest care label.
activity.evidence: Photos of the three pieces before and after sealing, plus your drying notes and label

lessons.title: Mixed media assemblage from found objects
objectives: Sort and clean found objects for use in art
Choose the right adhesive for each pair of materials
Compose an assemblage using focal point, repetition and balance
Build a framed piece that hangs securely

blocks.text: **Assemblage** is art made by arranging and fixing found objects onto a surface, often in a frame or shallow box. Bottle caps, broken jewellery, keys, wood off-cuts, ankara scraps, old watch parts, shells and calabash pieces all become materials. Done well, it produces original wall art and mirror frames that no factory can copy. Done badly, it looks like glued rubbish. The difference is composition and craftsmanship.

blocks.name: frame-with-picture
blocks.caption: An assemblage usually lives inside a frame or shallow box that holds it together visually.

blocks.text: Collecting and preparing materials

items: Sort finds by **material** (metal, wood, plastic, fabric, glass) and by **colour**. Keep them in labelled tins or bags.
Wash metal and plastic in soapy water and dry fully. Remove rust with sandpaper or a wire brush.
Check wood for termites or powdery holes; do not bring infested wood into your home.
Avoid sharp broken glass and anything that may have held chemicals, such as pesticide containers.
Flatten bottle caps with a hammer on a hard surface if you want flat discs; wear eye protection.

blocks.text: Adhesives: the right glue for the join

head: Adhesive
Good for
Not good for
Care
rows: Mix exactly as directed; ventilate; gloves
Burns skin; weak in strong heat

blocks.title: Fumes and burns
blocks.text: Solvent-based contact adhesives are flammable and give off strong fumes: use them outdoors or with windows open, away from stoves and candles, and close the tin after use. Hot glue guns reach temperatures that burn skin; rest the gun on its stand and keep a bowl of cold water nearby for accidental burns.
Composition that works

Before any glue, lay everything out on the backing board and photograph each arrangement. Look for a **focal point**: one object larger, brighter or more unusual than the rest, placed off-centre, often about one third in from an edge. Use **repetition** to tie the piece together, for example a row of the same bottle caps or a colour that appears in three places. Leave some **empty space** so the eye can rest. Odd numbers of similar objects (3, 5, 7) usually look more natural than even pairs.

blocks.title: Composition check before gluing
items: One clear focal point
Repeated colour or shape
Some empty space
Balanced visual weight
Photographed and compared
blocks.caption: Tick every item on the dry layout before anything is glued down.

blocks.title: Worked example: a bottle-cap sunburst mirror
blocks.context: For example, Joy in Warri makes a sunburst mirror frame from a collection of 120 bottle caps and a round mirror 20 cm across, on a 50 cm plywood circle.
steps: She cuts the plywood circle, sands the edge and paints it black so gaps between caps look intentional.
She glues the mirror in the centre with mirror adhesive (not solvent glue, which can damage the silver backing).

Her caps are about 3 cm across. She works out each ring from its circumference: ring 1, centred 12 cm from the middle, is 2 x 3.14 x 12 = about 75 cm, so 75 / 3 = 25 caps; ring 2 at 15.5 cm is about 97 cm, so 32 caps; ring 3 at 19 cm is about 119 cm, so 39 caps. Total: 25 + 32 + 39 = 96 caps.
She lays 96 caps out dry, choosing from her 120 so she can swap colours until the gold caps form evenly spaced 'rays', and photographs it.
She fixes each cap with two-part epoxy, working one ring at a time, then screws two D-rings and a picture wire to the back.
blocks.result: A 50 cm sunburst mirror with an even ray pattern, hung securely from D-rings and wire rather than glue alone.

blocks.text: Hanging securely

Heavy assemblages need fixings attached mechanically, not just glued: screw D-rings into the frame about one third of the way down from the top on each side and join them with picture wire. Weigh the finished piece on a kitchen or bathroom scale and tell the buyer the weight, so they choose a suitable wall plug and screw. Run a hand over the front and edges to check no sharp metal edges stick out.

Think about weight and depth from the start. A shallow box frame 3 to 5 cm deep protects raised objects and gives clean shadows when lit from the side. Glue the heaviest items low and near the centre line so the piece hangs straight, and keep loose, delicate parts such as chains or feathers away from the edges, where they get knocked during delivery.
Keep a short story card with each piece: what it is made from and where the materials came from. Buyers of upcycled art often value that story as much as the object.

takeaways: Sort, clean and check found objects before using them
Match the adhesive to the materials; use screws for heavy items
Lay out, photograph and compare before gluing
Hang with D-rings and wire and tell buyers the weight

activity.title: Mini assemblage
steps: Collect at least 20 small found objects and sort them by material and colour.
Lay out three different arrangements on a board or box lid and photograph each.
Choose the best one using the composition checklist and write why.
Fix the pieces with the correct adhesives and add a secure hanger.
