quiz.q: Wet cement splashes onto Kemi's forearm while mixing. What should she do?
options: Wash it off promptly with plenty of clean water
Wipe it off later when she finishes
Let it dry and peel it off
quiz.explain: Wet cement is alkaline and can burn skin, so it should be washed off promptly with plenty of water.

quiz.q: A cast planter came out weak, dusty and cracked. Which mistake most likely caused it?
options: Keeping it damp for a week
Too much water in the mix and drying fast in the sun
Tapping the mould to remove bubbles
quiz.explain: A wet mix plus fast drying weakens cement; it needs a porridge-like mix and damp curing.

quiz.q: Using 1 cement : 2 sand, how much sand goes with 1.5 litres of cement?
quiz.explain: Sand is twice the cement volume: 2 x 1.5 = 3 litres.

quiz.q: A customer wants an air-dry clay vase for fresh roses. What should you offer?
options: Seal it and fill it with water directly
Bake it in a kitchen oven to make it waterproof
Use more glue in the clay
Fit a glass or plastic tube inside to hold the water
quiz.explain: Air-dry clay is never waterproof, so water must be held in a separate insert.

quiz.q: Which adhesive suits fixing metal bottle caps to plywood for a heavy mirror frame?
quiz.explain: Epoxy bonds metal to wood strongly; PVA and hot glue are too weak for heavy, non-porous items.

quiz.q: Two clay pieces separated at the join while drying. What step was likely missed?
options: Scoring both surfaces and adding a little water or PVA
quiz.explain: Scoring and wetting both surfaces lets them bond; without it, shrinkage pulls joins apart.

modules.title: African Textile Dyeing and Printing
modules.overview: Colour on cloth is at the heart of Nigerian décor, from kampala tie-dye to Yoruba adire. This module teaches fibre-reactive tie-dye, the three main adire resist methods, how to dye larger home textiles evenly by weight, and how to fix, wash and label dyed work so the colour lasts.

lessons.title: Tie-dye with fibre-reactive dyes: folds, ties and fixing
objectives: Choose fabrics and dyes that bond permanently
Fold and tie spiral, bullseye, stripe and crumple patterns
Prepare soda ash and dye solutions safely
Batch, rinse and wash out a tie-dyed piece correctly

blocks.text: Tie-dye, often called **kampala** in Nigeria, works by **resist**: wherever fabric is tightly folded, tied or pressed, less dye reaches it, so it stays lighter. Many local dyers use vat dyes with caustic soda and sodium hydrosulphite. This lesson teaches a method that is easier to control at home and well documented by dye suppliers: **fibre-reactive dyes** fixed with **soda ash**, used cold on cotton.

blocks.name: t-shirt
blocks.caption: Cotton T-shirts and pillowcases are ideal first pieces for fibre-reactive tie-dye.

blocks.text: The right fabric and dye

Fibre-reactive dyes form a chemical bond with **plant fibres**: cotton, linen, rayon (viscose) and hemp. They do not dye polyester, and a polyester-cotton blend comes out pale. Old cotton bedsheets, T-shirts and plain shirting cloth bought by the yard are good, cheap materials. Wash new fabric first in hot water with detergent to remove factory finishes that block dye.
Four classic folds

items: **Spiral**: lay fabric flat, pinch the centre, twist into a flat round disc and tie with 3 or 4 rubber bands crossing in the middle like slices of a pie. Apply a different colour to each slice.
**Bullseye**: pinch the centre, pull up into a cone and tie bands at intervals down the cone. You get concentric rings.
**Stripes**: fold back and forth like a paper fan (accordion), then tie bands across. Fold straight for straight stripes or diagonally for diagonal stripes.
**Crumple (scrunch)**: scrunch the fabric randomly into a flat cake and tie it. Gives a marble-like texture, good for cushion covers.

blocks.title: Fibre-reactive tie-dye process
items: Pre-wash cotton
Soak in soda ash
Fold and tie
Apply dye
Batch 24 hours warm
Rinse cold, then wash
blocks.caption: The soda ash soak and the 24-hour wait are what make the colour permanent.

blocks.text: Preparing solutions

items: **Soda ash soak**: soda ash (sodium carbonate) raises the pH so the dye can bond. Dye suppliers commonly recommend about 1 cup of soda ash per gallon (about 3.8 litres) of warm water. Dissolve, soak fabric for 15 to 20 minutes, then wring out until damp, not dripping.

**Dye solution**: wearing a dust mask and gloves, mix dye powder into a little warm water to a paste, then top up. A common squeeze-bottle strength is about 2 teaspoons of dye per cup of water for most colours, and more for black or very dark shades. Always check your supplier's chart.
**Apply**: squeeze dye onto the tied fabric section by section, pressing it into the folds. Turn it over and dye the back if you want full coverage.
**Batch**: wrap the wet piece in nylon so it stays damp and keep it somewhere warm for about 24 hours. In most of Nigeria room temperature is warm enough; in harmattan nights, keep it in a warm room.

blocks.title: Dust, alkali and utensils
blocks.text: Dye powders are fine and can irritate lungs and cause allergies, so wear a dust mask when measuring powder and mix where there is no breeze. Soda ash irritates skin and eyes: wear gloves and avoid splashes. Keep all dyeing cups, spoons and buckets for dyeing only, never for food, and store powders labelled, sealed and out of reach of children.

blocks.title: Worked example: six spiral T-shirts for a family event
blocks.context: For example, Ifeoma in Onitsha dyes six white 100% cotton T-shirts in green and gold for a family reunion.
steps: She washes the shirts in hot water with detergent and hangs them until just damp.
She dissolves 1 cup of soda ash in about 3.8 litres of warm water and soaks all six shirts for 20 minutes, then wrings them out.
She twists each shirt into a spiral and ties it into 6 sections with rubber bands.
She mixes two squeeze bottles, each about 2 teaspoons of dye in 1 cup of water, and alternates green and gold around the 6 sections.
She wraps each shirt in nylon and leaves them 24 hours, then rinses in cold water until the water runs nearly clear, removes the bands, and washes them together in hot water with a little detergent.
blocks.result: Six matching spiral shirts with clear green and gold sections. Very little colour runs in the final wash because she rinsed thoroughly first.

blocks.text: Rinsing out correctly

After batching, the fabric holds both bonded dye and loose dye that never bonded. If you open a wet piece and wash it in warm water straight away, loose dye can spread into white areas. Rinse first in **cold water**, with the ties still on, until the water runs fairly clear. Then remove ties and continue rinsing. Finally wash in **hot water** with detergent to remove the last loose dye, and dry in shade. You will learn a full colourfastness test in Lesson 4 of this module.

blocks.title: Keep a dye diary
blocks.text: For every batch, write the fabric, soda ash amount, dye colours and teaspoons per cup, batch time, and a cut sample of the result. After ten batches you will be able to repeat any colour a client orders.

Pricing tie-dye sets depends on matching: a client ordering twelve shirts for an event expects them to look alike. Dye the full order in one session with one batch of mixed dye, rather than spread over several days.

takeaways: Fibre-reactive dyes bond with cotton and other plant fibres, not polyester
Soda ash soak plus about 24 warm hours fix the colour
Rinse cold before untying, then wash hot
Dust mask, gloves and dedicated utensils every time

activity.title: Four-fold sampler
steps: Cut four squares of about 40 cm from a pre-washed cotton sheet.
Soak in soda ash solution and wring out.
Tie one spiral, one bullseye, one stripe and one crumple.
Dye, batch for 24 hours, rinse and wash correctly.
Record everything in your dye diary.
activity.evidence: Photo of the four finished squares with their dye diary entries

lessons.title: Adire: oniko, alabere and eleko resist methods
objectives: Explain the meaning and history of adire in Yoruba textile tradition
Make oniko (tied), alabere (stitched) and eleko (starch paste) resists
Dip in an indigo-type vat correctly and recognise oxidation
Use traditional motifs respectfully in modern home décor

blocks.text: **Adire** is the indigo-dyed resist cloth of the Yoruba people of south-west Nigeria. The name is commonly explained as coming from **adi** (to tie) and **re** (to dye or soak). Abeokuta is often called the capital of adire making, with Ibadan and Osogbo also important centres. The craft grew in the early twentieth century when imported plain cotton shirting became widely available, declined later, and has been revived by artists and designers including Nike Davies-Okundaye.

blocks.name: spool-of-thread
blocks.caption: In alabere, stitches pulled tight before dyeing become the white pattern.

blocks.text: Three resist methods

head: Method
Resist
How it is done
Typical look
rows: Small objects such as seeds or pebbles are tied into the cloth, or sections are bound tightly
White circles and rings on blue
Lines of running stitch or folded-edge stitch are sewn, then gathered tight
Fine lines, stripes and leaf shapes
Paste is painted on by hand or pressed through a cut metal stencil, then dried

blocks.text: Named eleko motifs include **Olokun**, linked with the goddess of the sea, **Ibadandun** ('Ibadan is sweet') and the **jubilee** pattern, among many others. When you use these motifs commercially, describe them correctly and credit the tradition. Better still, design your own motifs using the same methods, so your work is original.
Making each resist

items: **Oniko**: pinch a small point of cloth around a seed or pebble and wrap thread or raffia tightly around its base 6 to 10 times; knot it. Repeat in a grid or a scattered pattern.

**Alabere**: draw lines lightly in pencil, sew along them with strong thread in a running stitch about 5 mm long, leaving long tails. Pull every thread tight so the cloth gathers into firm pleats, and knot.

**Eleko**: cook a smooth, thick paste of cassava flour and water, cool it, and paint it onto stretched cloth with a brush or feather, or spread it through a stencil. Let it dry completely, usually a full day in sun or warm air.
Wet tied or stitched cloth in plain water before dyeing so the dye spreads evenly. For eleko, keep the cloth dry until it enters the dye.

blocks.title: Indigo dipping cycle
items: Dip gently
Lift out: greenish
Air: turns blue
Dip again for darker
blocks.caption: Indigo colours in the air, not in the bath, so depth of blue comes from repeated dips.

blocks.text: How indigo works

Indigo does not dissolve in plain water. In a dye **vat** it is changed into a soluble, yellow-green form using an alkali and a reducing agent. Traditional dyers use fermented indigo leaves and ash lye; modern small dyers often use synthetic indigo with caustic soda and sodium hydrosulphite. When the cloth comes out of the vat it looks **yellow-green**, and within minutes in the air it turns **blue** as the dye oxidises. One dip gives pale blue; several dips, with airing between, give the deep blue that adire is known for.

blocks.title: Vat chemicals
blocks.text: Caustic soda is corrosive and causes severe burns; sodium hydrosulphite reacts with moisture and gives off irritating gas. If you use them, follow the supplier's instructions exactly, wear goggles, rubber gloves and long sleeves, work outdoors, add chemicals to water slowly (never water onto dry caustic soda), and store powders sealed and dry, away from children. A beginner can start with a ready-made indigo kit or work alongside an experienced dyer.

blocks.title: Worked example: an alabere and oniko table runner
blocks.context: For example, Yewande in Abeokuta makes a 35 x 150 cm cotton runner for a client's dining table.
steps: She pre-washes the cotton and pencils 5 parallel lines along the length, 6 cm apart, leaving about 5.5 cm at each long edge: 4 gaps x 6 cm = 24 cm, and 35 - 24 = 11 cm, split into two 5.5 cm edges.
She stitches each line in running stitch and pulls the threads tight.
Between the lines she ties small oniko circles around seeds, every 10 cm along the runner.
She wets the cloth, dips it for about a minute, airs it until blue, and repeats for 4 dips in total.
She rinses, removes stitches and ties carefully with a seam ripper, then washes and irons it.
blocks.result: A runner with five fine white stitched lines and rows of small circles on deep blue, all from planned measurements.

blocks.text: Eleko paste softens in liquid, so dip eleko cloth briefly and let it dry or air between dips; long soaking lifts the paste and blurs the design. After the final dip and airing, soak the cloth in water and gently scrape or rub off the softened paste.

Modern décor uses adire beautifully as cushion covers, table runners, framed panels, lampshades and upholstery panels. A single strong motif panel framed on a wall, or a set of cushions in three different resist methods, makes a confident statement in a neutral room.

takeaways: Adire is Yoruba indigo resist cloth with strong roots in Abeokuta, Ibadan and Osogbo
Oniko ties, alabere stitches, eleko uses cassava starch paste
Indigo comes out green and turns blue in air; depth comes from repeated dips
Credit traditional motifs and handle vat chemicals with full protection

activity.title: Three-resist sampler
steps: Prepare three pieces of pre-washed cotton, each about 30 x 30 cm.
Make one oniko, one alabere and one eleko resist (a simple painted shape is enough).
Dye all three in an indigo vat or kit with at least 3 dips each, airing between dips.
Remove resists, wash and iron, and label each with its method.
activity.evidence: Photos of each sampler before dyeing and after finishing, with method labels

lessons.title: Dyeing curtains, cushions and table linen evenly
objectives: Identify fibre content before dyeing a household textile
Calculate dye, water and fabric quantities by weight
Dye large pieces evenly using immersion dyeing
Choose colours and fabrics that suit sunlight and washing

blocks.text: Dyeing home textiles is often an upcycling job: faded curtains, stained white tablecloths and dull cushion covers can all get a second life with a new colour. Larger items bring a new challenge, **even colour**. A blotchy curtain is hard to sell. Immersion dyeing, where the whole piece moves freely in a dye bath, gives the most even result, and accurate quantities by weight make results repeatable.

blocks.name: bed
blocks.caption: Bed linen, curtains and cushions can be refreshed and upcycled with an even immersion dye.

blocks.text: Check what the fabric is

Read the label first. If there is none, cut a small snippet from a hidden seam and do a careful **burn test** outdoors, holding the snippet with tweezers over a non-flammable dish, away from anything that can catch fire. Cotton and linen burn with a smell like burning paper and leave soft grey ash. Polyester melts, shrinks away from the flame and leaves a hard bead. Fibre-reactive dye will only work well on the cotton-type result. Curtains with a rubbery blackout backing or a shiny coating are not good candidates.
Working by weight of fabric

Professional recipes are written as a **percentage of the dry fabric weight**, called depth of shade. Weigh the dry item on a kitchen or bathroom scale. Roughly, light shades use about 0.5 to 1% dye, medium shades about 2%, and dark shades 4% or more, but each dye and supplier differs, so use their chart and your dye diary. The **liquor ratio** is the weight of water to fabric. Allowing about 20 to 30 litres of water per kilogram of fabric (about 20:1 to 30:1) lets the piece move freely. Salt and soda ash are added per litre of water following the supplier's instructions.

blocks.title: Worked example: four cushion covers in a medium shade
blocks.context: For example, Nneka in Owerri upcycles four faded cotton cushion covers. Together they weigh 800 g dry. She wants a medium terracotta.
steps: Dye: 2% of 800 g = 0.02 x 800 = 16 g of dye powder.
Water: at a 20:1 ratio, 800 g fabric needs 20 x 0.8 = 16 litres of water.
She checks her supplier's chart for salt and soda ash per litre and multiplies by 16 litres.
She dissolves the dye completely, adds it to the water with the salt, puts in the pre-wetted covers and stirs for the time on the chart before adding the dissolved soda ash.
She stirs often, every few minutes at first, for the full time on the chart, then rinses and washes as for tie-dye.
blocks.result: Four evenly dyed covers in one matching colour. Because she wrote down 2% and 20:1, she can repeat the shade for a fifth cover later.

blocks.title: Even colour checklist
items: Fabric pre-washed and wet
Dye fully dissolved
Enough water to move
Stir often, especially early
One batch for matching items
blocks.caption: Most patchy results come from skipping one of these steps.

blocks.text: Large pieces such as curtains

items: Weigh each curtain panel. If a panel is too big for your largest basin or drum, dye it alone and stir constantly rather than crowding it.
Remove hooks, rings and tape that could rust or resist dye; synthetic thread in seams may stay the old colour, which can look like a design detail.
Dye all panels for one window in one session from one batch of mixed dye, so they match.
Expect cotton to shrink slightly, especially if it has never been washed hot. Wash and measure first, and allow for it when making curtains to size.

blocks.title: Sun fades colour
blocks.text: Curtains take strong Nigerian sun every day, and many dyes fade in direct sunlight over time. Choose colours your supplier rates well for light fastness, suggest a lining to clients, and avoid promising that bright colours will never fade. Medium and darker shades usually show fading less than pale pastels.
Choosing colours for a room

Dyed textiles usually provide accent colour in a room. Pick one colour from a rug, painting or adire piece already in the room and repeat it in two or three textiles. Dye a small swatch first and look at it in the actual room in daylight and at night, because colours look different under warm LED bulbs. Keep the swatch pinned to your order sheet.

blocks.title: Big buckets, hot water
blocks.text: A bucket with 16 litres of water weighs about 16 kg. Fill it where you will use it, lift with bent knees or scoop water out first, and keep hot dye baths away from children. Dye outdoors or in a ventilated space, and wear gloves throughout.

Upcycled textiles sell better with a short note on the label: 'upcycled cotton, hand-dyed'. Be honest about any old stains that the dye covered but did not remove, since some may show faintly in certain light.

takeaways: Check fibre content first; polyester does not take fibre-reactive dye
Work by dry fabric weight: dye percentage and liquor ratio
Pre-wet, dissolve fully, give room to move and stir often
Dye matching items in one batch and warn clients about sun fading

activity.title: Dye one household textile
steps: Choose an item such as a pillowcase, tea towel or cushion cover and confirm its fibre.
Weigh it dry and calculate dye at your chosen depth of shade and water at 20:1.
Dye a small swatch first, then the item.
Record before and after photos and all quantities.
activity.evidence: Calculation sheet, swatch, and before and after photos of the item

lessons.title: Colourfastness, washing, care labels and safe disposal
objectives: Test a dyed item for colour bleeding and rubbing
Fix the main causes of poor colourfastness
Write clear, honest care instructions for buyers
Dispose of used dye baths and chemicals responsibly

blocks.text: Nothing damages a textile business faster than a client whose new cushion bled onto a white sofa. Professional dyers test every batch before it leaves the workshop. This lesson gives you simple home tests, the fixes for common problems, care labels buyers can follow, and responsible handling of leftover dye and chemicals.

blocks.name: bubbles
blocks.caption: A simple wash test with a white cloth tells you whether a dyed item is ready to sell.

blocks.text: Why colour runs

head: Cause
What you see
Fix next time
rows: Rinse cold until clear, then wash hot
Not enough soda ash or time
Colour keeps fading wash after wash
Correct soda ash amount and a full 24-hour warm batch
Check fibre first; use suitable dyes
Vat dye not fully oxidised or rinsed
Air longer between dips, rinse and wash well
Heat-set as the product label directs

blocks.text: Two simple tests

items: **Wash test**: put the dyed item, or a cut swatch, in a basin of warm water with a little detergent together with a small piece of white cotton. Leave 30 minutes, squeeze a few times, then compare the white cloth with an unused piece. Any staining means more washing out is needed.

**Rub test**: rub a dry white cotton cloth firmly back and forth on the dyed surface about 10 times, then repeat with a damp white cloth. Colour on the cloth means loose dye or unfixed surface colour.
Repeat the tests after any extra washing until the white cloth stays clean, or nearly so.

blocks.title: Batch release decision
items: Wash test
Rub test
Pass: label and sell
Fail: rewash and retest
Still failing: sell as seconds
blocks.caption: A batch only leaves your workshop after it passes both tests.

blocks.title: Worked example: a failed batch saved
blocks.context: For example, Aisha in Kano finishes 10 indigo-dyed napkins for a restaurant. In the rub test, the damp white cloth turns light blue.
steps: She checks her notes: she aired each dip for only 2 minutes, and gave a short final rinse.
She soaks all 10 napkins in clean water for an hour, then washes them in hot water with detergent twice, rinsing well each time.
She dries them in shade and repeats both tests on two napkins.
The white cloth now shows only a very faint tint on the damp rub, so she writes 'wash separately for the first few washes' on the care card.
blocks.result: The batch is released with an honest care card instead of being rushed out, and her process notes now say to air each dip longer and wash twice.

blocks.text: Writing care labels

A good care label is short and specific. Include fibre content, dye method if useful (hand-dyed, indigo, tie-dye), washing temperature, and clear instructions. For most hand-dyed cotton décor, sensible instructions are: wash separately or with similar colours, use cool or warm water and mild detergent, do not use bleach, dry in shade, iron on the reverse. Use the internationally recognised textile care symbols if you know them well, but always add words too, because many buyers do not read the symbols.

items: Sample label: 100% cotton cushion cover, hand-dyed adire. Wash separately in cool water. No bleach. Dry in shade. Iron on reverse. Cushion insert not included.
Sew a small fabric label into seams, or attach a card tag with a ribbon for items like table runners.
Add your business name and WhatsApp number so satisfied buyers can reorder.

blocks.title: Responsible disposal
blocks.text: Used dye baths can contain alkali, salt and dye. Never pour them into streams, open gutters, near wells or boreholes, or onto vegetable gardens. Let solids settle, dilute with plenty of water and pour into a toilet or a sewer drain connected to a proper soak-away or sewer, away from water sources. Return unused chemicals to sealed, labelled containers. Follow any rules your state environmental agency sets for small workshops.

Keep a batch number on every order sheet and care card, for example 'IND-2026-07'. If a buyer ever reports a problem, you can look up exactly what you did, fix the process, and reassure the customer with facts, which builds trust.

Store finished stock folded in clean cotton bags or wrapped in plain paper, out of direct sun, and never in damp nylon, which can trap moisture and cause mildew spots during the rainy season. Keep different colours separated by paper until they are fully dry and tested, because damp deep blues and reds can mark lighter pieces they touch.
For decorative pieces that will rarely be washed, such as framed adire panels or wall hangings, say so on the label: 'spot clean only with a damp cloth' protects both the piece and you.

takeaways: Most bleeding comes from loose dye that was not rinsed out
Wash test and rub test with white cotton before every release
Care labels need words, not only symbols
Never dispose of dye baths into streams, gutters or near wells

activity.title: Test, label and release
steps: Take one of your dyed pieces from this module and run the wash test and rub test.
Photograph the white test cloths next to an unused piece of the same white cotton.
If it fails, rewash and retest.
Write a care label and give the item a batch number.
activity.evidence: Photos of test cloths, your pass or fail decision, and the finished care label

quiz.q: Seun's tie-dyed polyester-cotton shirt came out very pale. Why?
options: Fibre-reactive dye bonds with cotton but not polyester
quiz.explain: Fibre-reactive dyes bond with plant fibres; the polyester part of a blend stays largely undyed.

quiz.q: An indigo-dipped cloth comes out of the vat yellow-green. What should the dyer do?
options: Throw it away; the vat has failed
Let it air so it oxidises to blue, then dip again for deeper colour
Wash it immediately in hot water
quiz.explain: Indigo is yellow-green in its soluble form and turns blue as it oxidises in air.

quiz.q: Which adire method uses cassava starch paste as the resist?
quiz.explain: Eleko uses a cooked starch paste painted on or applied through a stencil.

quiz.q: A tablecloth weighs 1.2 kg dry. At 2% depth of shade, how much dye is needed?
At a 25:1 liquor ratio, how much water for 600 g of fabric?
quiz.explain: 25 x 0.6 kg = 15 litres.

quiz.q: In the rub test, a damp white cloth turns blue. What is the best next step?
options: Rewash thoroughly, retest, and label honestly
Iron it hot to set the blue
quiz.explain: Colour on the cloth means loose dye; rewash, retest, and only then release with an honest care card.

quiz.q: Where may a used dye bath be poured?
options: Diluted, into a toilet or sewer drain away from wells
quiz.explain: Dye baths should go diluted into a proper sewer or soak-away system, never into open water, gutters, gardens or near wells.

modules.title: Upcycling Strategy, Pricing and Styling Services
modules.overview: The final module turns skills into income. You will learn to choose upcycling projects that are worth the effort, refinish a piece of furniture safely, price handmade décor so every sale makes a profit, sell and get paid safely, and offer styling services that use your own pieces.

lessons.title: Strategic upcycling: choosing and refinishing furniture
objectives: Judge whether a used item is worth upcycling using cost, effort and value
Inspect furniture for structural damage, pests and old paint hazards
Follow a correct clean, repair, sand, prime, paint and seal sequence
Record before and after costs to prove the value added

blocks.text: Upcycling means turning something old or discarded into something of **higher value**. Not every old item is worth the work. Strategic upcyclers choose pieces where a modest amount of effort and material creates a big jump in value, and pass on the rest. Used furniture markets, relocation sales, carpenters' off-cuts and items friends are throwing away are all good sources.

blocks.name: chair
blocks.caption: A solid old chair with a tired finish is a classic high-value upcycling project.

blocks.text: Choosing the right projects

blocks.title: Upcycling project matrix
items: Quick wins: do first
Big projects: plan carefully
Small extras: batch them
Avoid: walk away
blocks.caption: Prioritise high-value pieces; low-value, high-effort items rarely pay back the time.

blocks.text: Read the matrix as follows: the top row is high value added, the bottom row is low; the left column is low effort, the right column is high. A solid wood side table that only needs sanding and paint is a quick win. A sofa needing new foam and upholstery may be a big project worth planning. Turning jars into candle holders is a small extra to batch. A chipboard wardrobe with swollen, water-damaged panels is usually one to avoid.
Inspect before you buy

items: **Structure**: press down and rock the piece. Loose joints can be re-glued; cracked legs and swollen chipboard are hard to fix well.
**Pests**: look for small round holes, fine powder (frass) underneath, or mud tunnels that suggest termites. Do not bring infested furniture into a home or workshop.
**Material**: solid wood sands and repairs well. Chipboard and MDF swell if wet and cannot be sanded deeply. Laminate needs special primer.
**Old paint**: thick, layered old paint of unknown age may contain lead.

blocks.title: Lead in old paint
blocks.text: The World Health Organization warns that lead paint is a major source of lead exposure, especially harmful to children and pregnant women. Do not dry-sand, burn or heat-strip old paint of unknown age. Where you must remove it, wet-sand or use a chemical stripper outdoors following the label, wear a well-fitting dust mask and gloves, clean up with damp cloths rather than sweeping, and keep children and pregnant women away. If unsure, paint over a sound old finish after a light scuff instead of removing it.
The refinishing sequence

items: **Clean**: wash with warm water and detergent (or sugar soap) to remove grease and dirt; rinse and dry fully.
**Repair**: re-glue loose joints with wood glue and clamp or tie them overnight; fill holes and chips with wood filler.
**Sand**: start at 80 or 120 grit for rough areas, then 180 to 240 grit for a smooth finish, sanding with the grain.
**Prime**: use a primer that suits the surface, especially on bare wood, filler patches, laminate or metal.
**Paint**: two thin coats are better than one thick coat; follow the tin's recoat time.
**Seal**: protect tabletops and handles with clear varnish or polyurethane. Replace hardware such as knobs if needed.

blocks.title: Worked example: a bedside cabinet upcycled for sale
blocks.context: For example, Patience in Lagos buys a solid wood bedside cabinet with a scratched varnish for 8,000 naira at a used furniture market (all prices here are illustrative; check your own local prices).
steps: Materials: sandpaper 1,500, wood filler 2,000, primer and paint from tins she already has, using about 3,000 worth, varnish about 2,000, two new brass-look knobs 3,000. Total materials = 1,500 + 2,000 + 3,000 + 2,000 + 3,000 = 11,500 naira.
Total spend including the cabinet: 8,000 + 11,500 = 19,500 naira.
Time: 7 hours across three days (cleaning, sanding, two coats, varnish, hardware).
She lines the inside of the drawer with leftover adire fabric from Module 4, a detail buyers notice.
She photographs it before and after in the same spot and light.
blocks.result: She now knows her full material spend (19,500 naira) and time (7 hours), which she will use in the next lesson to set a price that pays for both.

blocks.title: Before and after photos sell upcycling
blocks.text: Always photograph a piece before you touch it, from the same angle and in the same light you will use for the after photo. Side-by-side photos show buyers the transformation and justify your price better than any caption.

Strategic upcyclers also build a **look**: for example, every piece in deep green with brass hardware and an adire accent. A consistent look makes your work recognisable on social media and lets clients order matching pieces. Keep a stock list of items waiting for work, and do not buy more than you can finish in a month, or your space fills with half-done projects.

Ventilation matters for paints and varnishes, especially solvent-based ones. Work outdoors or with windows open, keep flames away, and let pieces cure for the time on the tin before wrapping them, or wrapping material may stick to the finish.

takeaways: Upcycle where effort is modest and value added is high
Inspect structure, pests, material and old paint before buying
Clean, repair, sand, prime, paint, seal: in that order
Record every cost and hour, and take matching before and after photos

activity.title: Upcycling project file
steps: Find three possible items to upcycle and place each on the project matrix with a reason.
Choose one and inspect it using the four checks, writing notes.
Refinish it using the six-step sequence.
Record all costs and hours, and take matching before and after photos.
activity.evidence: Matrix notes, inspection notes, cost and time record, and before and after photos

lessons.title: Costing, pricing and selling handmade décor safely
objectives: Build a full cost from materials, labour and overheads
Set retail and wholesale prices and explain markup versus margin
Choose selling channels that suit décor products
Take payment and deliver fragile items safely

blocks.text: Many talented makers lose money without noticing, because they price by guesswork or copy someone else. A sound price covers **everything** it cost you to make the piece, pays you for your time, and leaves a profit to grow the business. This lesson builds a price step by step, then covers where to sell and how to get paid safely.

blocks.name: receipt
blocks.caption: Every price starts from a written record of real costs and real time.

blocks.text: The four parts of a price

blocks.title: How a price is built
items: Profit
Overheads share
Labour: hours x rate
Materials actually used
blocks.caption: Materials form the base; labour, overheads and profit sit on top, and none can be skipped.

items: **Materials**: everything used in the piece, including small items such as glue, sandpaper, tags and packaging. Use what you actually used, from your records.
**Labour**: hours spent x an hourly rate you set for yourself. Decide a fair rate based on what you could earn elsewhere for skilled work.

**Overheads**: costs of running the business that are not in one piece: data, electricity or fuel, transport to market, tools that wear out. A simple method is to add a percentage, for example 10 to 15%, to materials plus labour, and check it against your real monthly overheads.
**Profit**: money for the business to grow, save and survive slow months.

blocks.title: Worked example: pricing a macramé wall hanging
blocks.context: For example, Halima from Module 1 prices her 45 cm diamond hanging. Prices are illustrative assumptions for this example only.
steps: Materials: she assumes cord at 250 naira per metre and used about 44 m: 44 x 250 = 11,000. Dowel 1,500, hanging cord, tag and packaging 1,000. Materials = 13,500 naira.
Labour: about 3.1 hours x 2,000 naira per hour = 6,200 naira.
Profit at a 30% markup on cost: 0.30 x 21,670 = 6,501. Price = 21,670 + 6,501 = 28,171, which she rounds to 28,500 naira.
blocks.result: Her retail price is 28,500 naira. The profit of about 6,800 naira after rounding is about 24% of the price, so a 30% markup gives a margin of roughly a quarter.

blocks.text: Markup, margin and wholesale

**Markup** is profit as a percentage of cost. **Margin** is profit as a percentage of the selling price. They are not the same: a 30% markup is only about a 23% margin before rounding. Confusing them is a common way to underprice. If a shop or interior designer will resell your work, they need their own profit, so you offer a **wholesale price** below retail. A common convention is that the shop's retail price is around double the wholesale price, so your wholesale price must still cover your full cost plus some profit. If your full cost leaves no room for that, either make the piece faster, use materials more efficiently, or sell it only retail.
Where décor sells

head: Channel
Good for
Watch out for
rows: Repeat buyers, custom orders, local delivery
Reply quickly; keep catalogue prices current
Showing before and after, styled room photos
Needs regular posting and good photos
Touch-and-feel items like textiles and clay
Larger repeat orders and matching sets
Agree wholesale prices and deadlines in writing

blocks.title: Payment scams
blocks.text: Never release goods on the strength of an SMS or a screenshot of a transfer: fake alerts are common. Confirm the money has actually arrived by checking your bank or wallet app. Be wary of 'overpayments' where the buyer asks you to refund the difference. Payment links from providers such as Paystack, or POS payments through Opay or Moniepoint, give you a record. For custom work, take a deposit, often half, before you buy materials.
Packing fragile décor

Cement, clay and glass pieces break in transit when packed loosely. Wrap each item in paper or bubble wrap, fill every gap in the box with shredded paper or cloth off-cuts so nothing moves, mark the box 'Fragile, this way up', and photograph the packed box before handover. Agree in writing who pays if an item breaks with the dispatch rider or logistics company.

Compare your price with similar handmade pieces on Instagram, WhatsApp catalogues and at local fairs, but only after you know your own full cost. If similar items sell for less than your cost, do not simply cut your price: find what makes yours different (size, finish, adire detail, upcycled story) and say it clearly, or improve your process so the piece costs less to make.

Review prices every few months. When your materials cost goes up, your price must follow, or your profit quietly disappears. Keep a simple sheet with each product, its full cost, its price and its margin, and update it whenever a supplier changes a price.

takeaways: Price = materials + labour + overheads + profit
Markup is on cost; margin is on price; they are different numbers
Wholesale must still cover full cost plus some profit
Confirm payment in your app, never by SMS alone, and pack fragile items tightly

lessons.title: Styling rooms with your work: vignettes, staging and styling services
objectives: Style a shelf, table or bed vignette using height, grouping and texture
Stage a room for photos or for a short-let listing with handmade pieces
Package and price a styling service and a décor rental kit
Build a portfolio that shows your pieces in real rooms

blocks.text: A décor **stylist** arranges objects, textiles and plants so a space looks finished and inviting, for living, for photographs, or for selling and renting property. Unlike a full interior decorator, a stylist usually works with what is in the room plus a curated set of accessories. For a maker, styling is powerful: every job shows your macramé, cushions, planters and upcycled furniture in real rooms, which sells more of them. (For client briefs, floor plans and quotations, see the Interior Decoration Basics course.)

blocks.name: interior-design
blocks.alt: A person arranging furniture and décor in a room
blocks.caption: Styling places your handmade pieces where clients can see how they would live with them.

blocks.text: Building a vignette

A **vignette** is a small styled group of objects on a shelf, side table, console or tray. Strong vignettes share a few habits. Group objects in **odd numbers**, often three. Vary **height**, so the tops form a triangle: a tall item such as a vase with dried grass, a medium item such as a stack of books with a clay dish on top, and a low item such as a candle holder. Mix **textures**: smooth cement, soft macramé, glossy glaze, rough wood. Repeat one **colour** across the room in at least three places so it feels planned.

blocks.title: Vignette check
items: Odd-numbered group
High, medium, low heights
Three or more textures
Repeated accent colour
Breathing space around it
blocks.caption: Run this check, step back two metres, and remove one item if it feels crowded.

blocks.text: Room-by-room styling moves

items: **Living room**: hang art or a macramé piece so its centre is roughly at eye level and its width is about two thirds of the sofa below; group cushions in pairs plus one contrast cushion; add a tray on the coffee table to gather small items.
**Bedroom**: layer bedding with a throw folded across the lower third of the bed, two pillows and one or two dyed accent cushions; style the bedside with lamp, book and one small object.
**Dining**: a runner, a low centrepiece that does not block faces, and matching napkins.
**Shelves**: alternate vertical books, horizontal stacks and objects; leave about a third of each shelf empty; add one trailing plant up high.

blocks.text: Staging for photos and short-lets

Short-let apartment hosts, estate agents and small brands need rooms that photograph well. Staging means removing personal clutter, adding a few well-chosen accessories, and arranging furniture so the room looks spacious. Photograph from a corner at about chest height, in daylight with curtains open and lamps on, and keep vertical lines straight. Bring a **styling kit**: a set of cushions, throws, vases, planters, trays, a macramé hanging and a few books, all in a neutral palette with one or two accent colours, so it suits most rooms.

blocks.title: Worked example: a short-let styling package
blocks.context: For example, Zainab in Abuja offers to style a one-bedroom short-let flat for a host, mostly with pieces she made during this course. Figures are illustrative.
steps: Products sold to the host at her retail prices: one macramé hanging 28,500, four dyed cushion covers at 9,000 each = 36,000, two cement planters with plants at 12,000 each = 24,000, one upcycled bedside cabinet 38,000. Products total = 28,500 + 36,000 + 24,000 + 38,000 = 126,500 naira.
Styling labour: 1 hour site visit plus 5 hours styling on the day = 6 hours at 3,000 naira = 18,000 naira.
Transport for the visit and delivery: 8,000 naira.
Package total = 126,500 + 18,000 + 8,000 = 152,500 naira; she offers it as 150,000 if the host also allows her to use the photos in her portfolio.
She takes 50% deposit (75,000) to start, styles the flat, photographs every room, and collects the balance on completion.
blocks.result: The host gets a finished, photo-ready flat; Zainab sells six products in one job, earns for her time, and gains portfolio photos showing her pieces in a real room.

blocks.text: Décor rental

Some clients need décor for only a day or a weekend: an event, a shoot or a viewing. You can rent pieces from your styling kit for a fee plus a refundable **damage deposit**. Keep an inventory list with a photo of each item, check items out and back in with the client, and write down condition each time. Rental earns repeatedly from pieces you already own.

blocks.title: Agree photo rights
blocks.text: Before you photograph a client's home, ask permission in writing to use the photos in your portfolio and social media, and leave out house numbers, family photos and anything that reveals the address or personal details. Clients trust stylists who protect their privacy.

Your portfolio should show each piece close up and in a styled room, with a short caption: item, materials, size and price range. Group it by room so a client can picture their own space. Ten strong, well-lit projects persuade better than fifty quick phone snaps.

takeaways: Vignettes: odd numbers, varied heights, mixed textures, repeated colour
Staging removes clutter and adds a neutral styling kit with one or two accents
Package products, styling time and transport; take a deposit
Get written permission for photos and protect client privacy

quiz.q: Which item is the best 'quick win' to upcycle?
options: A solid wood side table with a worn finish
A sofa with collapsed springs and torn foam
A cabinet with fresh termite tunnels
quiz.explain: Solid wood with only surface wear needs modest effort for a big value gain.

quiz.q: A cabinet has thick, flaking old paint of unknown age. What is the safest approach?
options: Avoid dry sanding; wet-sand or strip outdoors with protection, or paint over a sound finish
Burn the paint off with a flame
Ask a child to help scrape it
quiz.explain: Old paint may contain lead; dry sanding and heating release dust and fumes that are especially harmful to children and pregnant women.

quiz.q: Materials 10,000, labour 5,000, overheads 1,500. With a 20% markup on full cost, what is the price?
quiz.explain: Full cost = 16,500; 20% markup = 3,300; price = 19,800.

quiz.q: Profit is 2,000 naira on a selling price of 10,000 naira. What is the margin?
quiz.explain: Margin is profit divided by price: 2,000 / 10,000 = 20%. (The markup on the 8,000 cost would be 25%.)

quiz.q: A buyer sends a screenshot of a transfer and asks for immediate dispatch. What should the maker do?
options: Check her bank or wallet app to confirm the money arrived
quiz.explain: Screenshots and SMS alerts can be faked; only the bank or wallet app confirms the funds.

quiz.q: Which group follows the vignette guidance best?
options: Two identical vases of the same height
A tall vase, a medium book stack with a clay dish, and a low candle holder
Seven small objects in a straight line
One large plant alone covering the whole shelf
quiz.explain: Three items with high, medium and low heights and mixed textures form a balanced triangle.

finalQuiz.q: A client wants a 70 cm long macramé hanging. Using the 4 times per strand rule with lark's head mounting, how long is each cut cord?
finalQuiz.explain: 70 x 4 = 280 cm per strand, doubled for the fold = 560 cm, or 5.6 m.

finalQuiz.q: A plant hanger basket must hold a pot 18 cm across. About what circumference must the cords wrap?
Which sequence gives decoupage the smoothest, edge-free finish?
options: Many thin coats with light wet sanding after several coats
finalQuiz.explain: Thin coats build up and gentle wet sanding flattens ridges until the edge disappears.

finalQuiz.q: Stencil paint keeps bleeding under the edges. What is the main fix?
options: Off-load the brush and pounce lightly in layers
finalQuiz.explain: Excess paint creeps under the stencil; an almost dry brush dabbed up and down keeps edges sharp.

finalQuiz.q: Joy mixes 1 cement to 2 sand. She has 3 litres of sand. How much cement does she need?
finalQuiz.explain: Cement is half the sand volume: 3 / 2 = 1.5 litres.

finalQuiz.q: A freshly demoulded cement planter is left in hot sun and harmattan wind for a week. What is the likely result?
options: A weaker, dusty surface that may crack
finalQuiz.explain: Cement needs to stay damp while it cures; fast drying weakens it.

finalQuiz.q: Which statement about air-dry clay and cold porcelain is correct?
options: They are not waterproof, so water and food need a separate insert
finalQuiz.explain: Air-dried pieces are never waterproof or food-safe, even when sealed.

finalQuiz.q: Which adire method uses stitching pulled tight before dyeing?
finalQuiz.explain: Alabere means stitched resist; the gathered stitches stay white.

finalQuiz.q: Curtains weigh 1.5 kg dry. At 4% depth of shade and a 20:1 liquor ratio, what dye and water are needed?
After tie-dye batching, what is the correct first rinse?
options: Untie and wash in hot water at once
Rinse in cold water with ties still on until it runs fairly clear
finalQuiz.explain: Cold rinsing first removes loose dye before it can spread into the white areas.

finalQuiz.q: Full cost of a stool is 24,000 naira and the price is 30,000 naira. What are the markup and margin?
A short-let host asks Zainab to style a flat and post the photos. What should she do about the photos?
options: Post everything, including the house number
Ask the host to take them
Get written permission and leave out anything revealing the address or personal details
finalQuiz.explain: Written permission and protecting privacy build trust and avoid harm.

capstone.title: Upcycled room collection and styling package
capstone.brief: Create a coordinated collection of at least five décor pieces for one room, using at least four techniques from different modules and at least two upcycled items, then cost, price and style them in a real room and present a sellable styling package.
steps: Choose a room (your own, a friend's or a client's) and a colour palette of a neutral plus one or two accents, with a reason.
Make at least five pieces using four techniques, for example a macramé hanging, stencilled or dyed cushion covers, a cement planter, a clay dish set and a refinished piece of furniture.
Keep a production record for each piece: materials used, quantities, time, and any safety steps.
Run the wash and rub tests on dyed textiles and load-test any hanging item; write care labels for every piece.
Complete a price sheet with full cost, retail price, markup and margin for each piece.
Style the room using the vignette check, and photograph before and after from the same spots.
Write a one-page styling package offer based on your collection, including deposit and payment terms.
evidence: Production record for five or more pieces showing four techniques and two upcycled items
Safety setup photos for cement and dyeing work
Before and after room photos with captions
